Recognise and use the formal prepositions with the genitive found in official texts and invitations.
Tell them apart from their colloquial equivalents (anlässlich = zu; bezüglich = wegen / über; mittels = mit).
Use the prepositions of place with the genitive: unweit, oberhalb, unterhalb, abseits, innerhalb, außerhalb.
Know when they are replaced in speech by “von + D” (unweit von Weimar).
It's August 2034. Jakob's mother has sent the invitation to the party in her village in Thuringia. It's written very formally. Ludwig and Lena are reading it at the café.
Grandpa, listen: “On the occasion of the marriage of our son Jakob to Mara Ionescu, we warmly invite you to a party in our garden.”
“Anlässlich”. Mrs Lorenz writes like a mayor. And then?
“The party will take place on Saturday, 19 August, from 2 p.m. In view of the expected heat, we kindly ask you to wear light clothing.”
In other words: it'll be hot, don't dress too warmly. Typical Thuringia. There you never say anything simply if you can say it in a complicated way.
It gets even better: “Regarding your arrival, we recommend the train to Weimar. Our village is not far from the town, about twenty minutes by bus.”
“Mittels Bus”! Ingrid would have underlined that in red. You go by bus, not by means of a bus.
And the last sentence: “Instead of gifts, we kindly ask you to make a donation for the benefit of the Pankow music school, in memory of Mr Friedrich Mertens.”
Oh. That's… that's lovely. That must have been Mara's idea.
Are you coming too, Grandpa? It's only three hours by train. Not twenty-four like to Sibiu.
Three hours is fine. And in view of the fact that Jakob wants to show me a fountain and a lime tree there that he's been talking about for five years, I can hardly say no.

2. Prepositions of place with the genitive
entlang des Flusses / den Fluss entlang
“entlang” is special: before the noun it takes the genitive (entlang des Flusses), after the noun the accusative (den Fluss entlang). Both are correct.

The village was called Lindenhain; it lay not far from Weimar, on a small plateau above the Ilm valley, and it had two hundred and forty inhabitants, a twelfth-century church, a baker who opened only on Tuesdays and Fridays, and a lime tree. The lime tree stood in the middle of the village square, next to an old stone fountain, and, as Mrs Lorenz proudly told everyone, it was more than three hundred years old. Under it, the people of Lindenhain had danced, quarrelled, got engaged and said goodbye for three hundred years. And under it Jakob's grandmother, Hilde, had sung the little boy the song about the fountain and the lime tree every summer evening.

Ludwig had come with Lena and Andrei, by train to Weimar and then on the bus that Mrs Lorenz had so solemnly called “mittels Bus” in the invitation. The bus was small, yellow and old; the driver was called Mr Schubert and knew every passenger by name, and when he heard that Ludwig had driven trams in Berlin for forty years, he let him sit at the front next to him the whole way and told him about the bends between Weimar and Lindenhain, which he had been driving for thirty years. When Ludwig got off, Mr Schubert said: “Colleague, when you go back, take the six o'clock bus. I'm driving that one too.”

Mrs Lorenz welcomed them at the garden gate, in a flowery apron, with flour on her hands and with a hug that almost knocked Ludwig's stick out of his hand. “Mr Brandt!” she cried. “The famous Mr Brandt! Jakob has told me so much about you that I feel I've known you for years.” She led him through the garden to a place of honour under the biggest apple tree, with a cushion on the chair and a glass of homemade elderflower lemonade. “In view of your age,” she said seriously, “you get the best seat. That's how it is with us. And in view of your charm, likewise.” Ludwig laughed so loudly that the neighbours looked over the fence.

The party was in Mrs Lorenz's garden, away from the main road, behind an old half-timbered house with green shutters. In view of the scorching heat, thirty-eight degrees as in Sibiu, the neighbours had put up sunshades and carried the tables under the apple trees. There were Thuringian sausages on the charcoal grill, Thuringian dumplings, potato salad in three versions, and cakes, so many cakes that Andrei, the baker, was lost for words for the first time in his life. Mrs Lorenz had baked twelve trays. Plum cake, poppy-seed cake, crumble cake, onion tart. “With us,” she explained, “a party without twelve cakes isn't a party. Regarding our tradition, that's not negotiable.”

Andrei tasted every single cake, with the serious face of an expert, and secretly noted down the recipes on a napkin. Mrs Lorenz saw and laughed. “You'll get them all,” she said. “On one condition: that you make me an onion tart to my recipe for the christening, in Berlin.” Andrei promised, without asking which christening she meant. Only later did he understand that she already knew.

The whole village had come, all two hundred and forty inhabitants, or so it seemed, half of them at any rate. The mayor, who was also the baker. The pastor, a woman, who came on a moped. Three old women who had known Jakob as a little boy with a cello and took turns pinching his cheeks. And Mr Schubert, the bus driver, who dropped by for half an hour between two runs, ate a sausage, discussed braking distances with Ludwig and then left again, punctual to the minute. Ludwig watched him go and said to Lena: “You see. There are good drivers everywhere. You recognise them by the fact that they're never late and never leave too early.”

Jakob sat next to Mara all afternoon and held her hand under the table, and Ludwig noticed that Mara drank none of the wine Mr Schubert had brought, nor the elderflower schnapps the mayor offered to anyone who didn't refuse quickly enough. She drank water. She ate two slices of onion tart, then a third, then a fourth, and Mrs Lorenz watched her with narrowed eyes, the way Grete looked at Elif when she was playing the piano and had noticed something, but didn't want to say anything yet.

In the evening, when the heat had eased and the shadows of the apple trees had grown longer, Jakob took Ludwig by the arm and led him, slowly, leaning on his stick, along the village street to the village square. Mara came too, and Lena and Andrei, and Mrs Lorenz, and in the end almost half the party was following them, glasses in hand, as if they all knew something was about to happen. Under the lime tree, Jakob stopped. The fountain was splashing. The light of the setting sun fell golden through the leaves. And Jakob said: “Here, Ludwig. This is the lime tree. And this is the fountain. The ones the song is about.”

Ludwig looked up at the huge crown of the lime tree, which was so wide that it shaded half the square. He thought of the song Jakob had played a year earlier in Kollwitzpark, on the cello, with trembling hands. He thought of Hilde, whom he had never known, and of Ingrid, whom he had known for so long, and of how people who have never met are sometimes strangely connected to each other, by a song, a tree, a ring. “Three hundred years,” he said quietly. “How many stories this tree must know.”

Ludwig, it's about to know one more. I haven't even told Jakob. I wanted to say it here. Under this lime tree. Because Jakob told me that the most important things have been said here for three hundred years.

The village square went very quiet. Jakob turned to Mara, with a face on which something was slowly changing, the way the sky changes just before the sun rises. Mara took his hand and put it on her belly, under the light summer dress she was wearing because of the heat. And she said, in German and then in Romanian, so that everyone would understand, including Andrei, who had already guessed: “I'm pregnant. In February. The doctor said around the twentieth of February.”

Jakob said nothing. He couldn't say anything. He lifted Mara up in his arms, in the middle of the village square of Lindenhain, under the three-hundred-year-old lime tree, and spun round with her, the way it happens in films and almost never in real life. Mrs Lorenz screamed so loudly that the pigeons in the village church took flight. Lena was crying. Andrei hugged his sister so tightly that she protested. And half the village, who had come along with their glasses in hand without knowing why, applauded, and someone, probably the mayor, who was also the baker, began to sing the song about the fountain and the lime tree, and everyone sang along.

Ludwig didn't sing. He didn't know the song well enough. But he stood under the lime tree, leaning on his stick, and watched Jakob put Mara down and take her face in both hands, and thought of an evening in May 1975, of a tram stop under a chestnut tree, of a young woman with a bunch of white chestnut blossoms. Some things, he thought, always happen under trees. He didn't know why. Perhaps because trees live longer than people and so they know how to listen better.

Later in the evening, when the street lamps had come on in the village square and most people had gone back to the garden, Ludwig stayed sitting alone on the bench by the fountain. Mrs Lorenz sat down next to him with two glasses of elderflower lemonade, and for a while neither of them said anything. Then she told him about her mother, Hilde, who had sat on this bench every evening until she was ninety and who had said she wouldn't die until Jakob had found the right girl. “She died before she met Mara,” Mrs Lorenz said quietly. “Five years too early. But today, under the lime tree, I had the feeling that she was sitting here next to us and saying: you see. I knew it all along.”

The next morning, at breakfast in the garden, Mara sat down next to Ludwig while the others were still asleep. She had a cup of tea in her hand and looked tired and happy. “Ludwig,” she said, “Jakob and I talked about names last night. If it's a girl, we'd like to call her Ingrid. Ingrid Hilde. After the two women we never knew and who brought us together all the same. Would that be all right with you?” Ludwig put his cup down, very slowly. He looked out over the garden, over the apple trees, at the church spire above the roofs. Then he said a single word, in a voice that wasn't quite steady: “Yes.”

The next evening, at six, Ludwig got on the little yellow bus again. Mr Schubert was at the wheel, punctual to the minute. “Well?” he asked. “How was the party?” Ludwig sat down at the front next to him, put his stick between his knees and looked out of the window at the village lying in the evening sun, at the church above the houses, at the crown of the lime tree, which could still be seen from far away. “It was,” he said, “on the occasion of a wedding. And it turned into a birth.” Mr Schubert didn't quite understand what he meant. But he smiled, put the bus into gear and set off, slowly, very slowly, because he saw that his passenger hadn't finished looking out of the window yet.
